Gnosis
NOH-sis
n. (Greek)
Greek gnōsis, “knowledge,” from ginōskō (to know); distinct from epignōsis (full or precise knowledge, often used in the NT for the recognition-knowledge of salvation).

Biblical Definition

Gnōsis in the New Testament is one of the chief words for knowledge—a category that carries great theological weight in apostolic teaching about what the saint knows of God, of Christ, of salvation, of himself, and of the truth. Paul ranks knowledge among the abundances he ascribes to the Corinthian church: ye are enriched by him, in all utterance, and in all knowledge (1 Cor 1:5). He lists knowledge among the gifts of the Spirit: to another faith by the same Spirit; to another the gifts of healing by the same Spirit; To another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues. But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will (1 Cor 12:9-11). The supreme value he sets upon a particular knowledge: yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ (Phil 3:8). The knowledge Paul prizes is not abstract information but the relational and saving knowledge of the Christ who has loved him and given Himself for him. Peter sets the growth-keynote of the Christian life around the same word: but grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ (2 Pet 3:18). And the great theological doxology in Romans 11 honors the immensity of God’s own knowledge: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! (Rom 11:33). The biblical doctrine of gnōsis has therefore both an exalted and a cautionary side. Exalted: the saint is to grow in the knowledge of Christ; the church is to be enriched in all knowledge; the depth of God’s wisdom and knowledge is worthy of doxology. Cautionary: knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth (1 Cor 8:1)—knowledge alone, divorced from love, inflates the knower rather than edifying him; and the heretical movement of the second-century church that would self-designate as Gnostics (claimants of special saving knowledge inaccessible to ordinary believers) is already prefigured in Paul’s warning to Timothy against oppositions of science (gnōsis) falsely so called (1 Tim 6:20). Biblical gnōsis is therefore the relational, saving, growing knowledge of God in Christ—held with humility, married to love, anchored in the apostolic deposit, and aimed at the doxology that the depth of God’s own knowledge invites.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines KNOWLEDGE as a clear perception of fact, truth, or duty; in scripture (rendering the Greek gnōsis), the relational and saving knowledge of God in Christ that the saint is to grow in, paired with love that the knowledge may not inflate.

expand to see more

KNOWLEDGE, n. — 1. A clear and certain perception of that which exists, or of truth and fact. 2. Learning; illumination of mind. 3. Acquaintance with any fact or person. 4. Cognizance; notice. 5. In scripture, the relational and saving knowledge of God in Christ; the gift of the Spirit (1 Cor 12:8); the excellency for which all else is counted loss (Phil 3:8).

GNOSIS — (Greek term) Knowledge; especially used in 1 Cor 8:1; 12:8; 13:2, 8; 14:6; 2 Cor 6:6; 8:7; 10:5; 11:6; Eph 3:19; Phil 3:8; Col 2:3; 2 Pet 1:5-6; 3:18.

Key Scripture

Philippians 3:8 — "Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord."

2 Peter 3:18 — "But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be glory both now and for ever. Amen."

Romans 11:33 — "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!"

1 Corinthians 8:1 — "Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth."

Modern Corruption

Gnōsis is corrupted, on one side, by the ancient and recurring Gnostic heresy that treats saving knowledge as a special elite possession inaccessible to ordinary believers—and on the other by the knowledge-puffs-up pattern Paul warns against, in which doctrinal precision is held without the love that would edify and produces the inflated knower rather than the built-up believer.

expand to see more

The Gnostic corruption is the most historically significant counterfeit of gnōsis. Second-century movements claiming a special saving knowledge inaccessible to ordinary believers—passed through initiation, taught by esoteric teachers, divorced from the apostolic deposit—produced what the early church recognized and refuted as a fundamental departure from the gospel. Paul’s charge to Timothy is the canonical warning: O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science (gnōsis) falsely so called (1 Tim 6:20). Biblical knowledge is not esoteric: it is the apostolic deposit set forth in the Scriptures and applied by the Spirit to every regenerate saint. The recovery against every recurrence of the Gnostic pattern (in second-century forms, in medieval mystical movements, in modern esoteric Christianity) is the same: the knowledge that saves is the knowledge of Christ as set forth in the public apostolic deposit, available to every believer through the Word and the Spirit.

The opposite corruption, more visible in the contemporary church, is the knowledge-puffs-up pattern Paul warns against in 1 Corinthians 8. Doctrinal precision is held without the love that would edify; the saint becomes more careful about doctrine and less charitable in his dealings; the very knowledge that should produce humility (the more I know of Christ, the more I see what I am) produces instead an inflated sense of one’s spiritual achievement. Paul’s remedy is precise: knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth. The cure is not less knowledge but more love—the love that, married to the knowledge, builds up both the knower and his brothers. Recover both ends. Refuse the Gnostic substitution of esoteric special knowledge for the apostolic public deposit, and refuse the knowledge-without-love pattern that inflates the knower. The biblical gnōsis is the relational, saving, growing knowledge of God in Christ, held with humility, married to love, anchored in the apostolic Word—and the church saturated with such knowledge is the church both well-instructed and visibly humble in the depth of what she has come to know.

Hebrew Roots

Greek gnōsis (knowledge) from ginōskō (to know); cousin term epignōsis (full or precise knowledge); set against the Gnostic counterfeit (esoteric special knowledge) and the knowledge-puffs-up pattern (precision without love).

expand to see more

Greek gnōsis (G1108) — knowledge (1 Cor 1:5; 8:1; 12:8; 13:2, 8; 14:6; 2 Cor 6:6; 11:6; Eph 3:19; Phil 3:8; Col 2:3; 1 Pet 3:7; 2 Pet 1:5-6; 3:18).

Greek ginōskō (G1097) — to know, perceive, understand (the verb).

Greek epignōsis (G1922) — full or precise knowledge, recognition (Eph 1:17; 4:13; Phil 1:9; Col 1:9-10; 1 Tim 2:4; 2 Tim 2:25; Heb 10:26; 2 Pet 1:2-3, 8; 2:20).

Hebrew da‘ath (H1847) — knowledge (Prov 1:7; 2:6; Isa 11:9; Hos 4:6).

Usage

"The excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord—Paul counts all things loss for this relational saving knowledge."

"Grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ—Peter sets the Christian life’s growth around the same word."

"Gnostic counterfeit makes saving knowledge esoteric; knowledge-puffs-up pattern divorces precision from love; biblical gnōsis is the apostolic public knowledge of Christ held with humility and married to love."
